t: LeetCode 2060 - Check if an Original String Exists Given Two Encoded Strings: Tracking the Length Difference
o: **Understanding the problem.** An unknown lowercase string was encoded twice, possibly with different splits: pieces left as text stay letters, chosen pieces were replaced by their decimal lengths, and each encoding concatenates the results. We must decide whether at least one original string produces both s1 and s2. Example 1: "internationalization" splits so its middle 18 letters collapse into the token 18, giving "i18n", so the answer is true. Example 2: "l123e" comes from ["l", "e", "et", "cod", "e"] with the middle pieces replaced by their lengths, while "44" comes from ["leet", "code"] - both descend from "leetcode". Example 3 fails because "a5b" forces the original to start with a while "c5b" forces c. Since lengths are at most 40 and digit runs are at most 3 long, each run hides one number from 1 to 999 readable in at most three ways - a perfect fit for a joint scan over both strings that remembers which side is currently ahead in original-length terms.
k: Track d = original length represented by the consumed prefix of s1 minus that of s2; the two encodings are synchronized exactly when d = 0.
A run of up to 3 digits is ambiguous: it may be read as a 1-, 2-, or 3-digit number, so branch on every parse.
Letters can be compared only when d = 0; otherwise consume an element from whichever string is behind.
Memoizing on (i, j, d) is effective because lengths of at most 40 keep the reachable state space small.

a.i: Walk through both encodings together carrying d, the gap between the original lengths the two consumed prefixes stand for. Whenever one side is ahead, feed the lagging side; whenever aligned, either match two letters or expand a digit run into a concrete number. Trying every choice without caching is the direct translation of the problem statement.
s: Recurse on (i, j, d): d equals characters represented by s1[0..i) minus those represented by s2[0..j).
If both pointers reached the ends, return d == 0.
If d > 0, s1 leads: consume one s2 element - a letter subtracts 1, each numeric parse subtracts its value; mirror this for d < 0.
If d = 0 and both next characters are letters, require equality and advance both; otherwise branch over every reading of the digit run on either side.
a.t: Exponential, up to O(6^(n+m)) worst case - each state spawns up to six branches and states repeat

a.n: Approach 2: Top-Down DP on (Index, Index, Difference)
a.i: The uncached recursion recomputes identical triples (i, j, d) over and over. Caching one verdict per triple reduces the work to the number of distinct reachable states times a constant transition cost. Runs of at most three digits cap per-state branching.
s: Wrap the recursion in a hash map keyed by the triple (i, j, d).
Return cached verdicts immediately; store each verdict after computing it.
Enumerate numeric parses by taking 1, 2, then 3 leading digits of a run as a single number.
a.t: O(n * m * D) - each combination of both pointers with the D reachable difference values is solved once with O(1) parse work
a.sp: O(n * m * D) - the memo table plus the recursion stack

w: Present the alignment idea first: prefixes can only describe one common string when the represented lengths coincide. Classic pitfalls: forgetting that a digit run has several readings (try the 1-, 2-, and 3-digit parses), comparing letters while misaligned, and botching base cases when exactly one string is exhausted. The memo stays compact because d only takes values expressible as partial sums of parsed numbers. Likely follow-ups: count the common originals instead of deciding existence, or reconstruct one witness string.
